html:
SMTO-API-0010 — What you sent is too large for SMTO to accept

GUID: 34e86a28-1af8-4840-a139-df99370db2d9
Slug: api-payload-too-large
Domain: API · Subsystem: api

What happened

  • SMTO turned down this request because it was bigger than allowed, such as a large attached file, a big export, or very long text in a setting.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Read What the server reported in this panel; it usually names the limit, such as a largest allowed file or request size. Knowing the exact limit tells you how much smaller each part needs to be.
  2. For an attachment, make the file smaller, for example by compressing it or splitting it into parts, and attach each part separately. Each file has to fit under the attachment size limit on its own.
  3. For an export, upload or file selection, choose fewer items at a time and repeat for the rest. Smaller batches stay under the limit while still covering everything.
  4. If you regularly need larger attachments, ask the person who manages SMTO about Maximum attachment size in Settings › Operate › Execution. That setting controls how large each uploaded file can be.

What success looks like

  • Each smaller part is accepted, and everything you meant to send arrived.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them, with the size of what you were sending, to the person who manages SMTO. Don't delete saved files or conversations to make room; that doesn't raise this limit.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • An SMTO or Gateway endpoint rejected the request body with HTTP 413 because it exceeded that route's size limit (for example attachment size, export archive size, a 1 MiB certificate request, a workspace file or upload limit, a Knowledge document, or a 64 KiB Skill management request).

What this means

  • HTTP enrichment maps an otherwise unclassified status 413 to the payload-size category. Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.

Why this can happen

  • HTTP enrichment maps an otherwise unclassified status 413 to the payload-size category.

How to diagnose it

  • Check the route's actual payload limit and encoded request size; this category does not identify which component enforced it.

How to fix it

  • Read the response detail for the specific limit, then reduce or split the request to fit it without silently truncating content. If the limit is too low for legitimate use, raise attachment_max_file_bytes (Settings › Operate › Execution › Maximum attachment size) or the relevant route limit.
  • Reduce or split the submitted payload to the supported limit.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • A complete supported payload fits the owning route's limit without silent truncation.

What not to do

  • Do not erase authoritative receipts or protected current input to conceal a size/capacity problem.

Technical notes

  • Generic API status and exception families establish only their stated boundary. Stronger structured causes take precedence; the original receipt determines whether work started or had effects, and diagnostics add no dispatch or retry.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
